tldr: By explicitly estimating unknown disturbances like payloads and external forces online as a single quantity in joint space, and using them for both feedforward torque compensation and policy observation augmentation, PACE achieves an 11.5 kg payload (nearly its own mass) and 16 cm step-downs trained exclusively on flat ground in simulation.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the PACE framework. (a) In the training phase, the explicitly estimated disturbance torque is routed to low-level torque compensation while also being fed into the policy network as an observation. (b) During real-world deployment, contact forces are estimated from onboard sensors without foot force sensors, running an observer identical in structure to training.
overview:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has driven remarkable progress in quadrupedal locomotion. However, handling unmodeled disturbances in the real world—such as payloads, center-of-mass (CoM) shifts, actuator degradation, and external forces from uneven terrain—remains a major challenge. The standard approach is domain randomization (heavily varying physical parameters during training). But this forces the policy to adopt overly conservative motions that hedge against every condition. As a result, velocity-tracking accuracy drops, and handling large changes outside the sampled range remains difficult.

To tackle this, the authors asked: instead of lumping disturbances into a black-box latent variable, why not explicitly estimate them online as physical disturbance torques in joint space? In the proposed method, PACE, they introduce a nonlinear disturbance observer (DO) that recovers disturbances without joint acceleration measurements, avoiding derivative noise. Here is the key: this estimated disturbance is not only applied directly as feedforward compensation to the PD controller torque, but is also fed into the high-level policy as an augmented observation. Furthermore, by embedding this observer into the training loop from the beginning, the policy learns optimal actions in a world where disturbances are already compensated.

Evaluated on a real robot (DeepRobotics Lite3, self-mass ~11.6 kg) and in physics simulation, the policy was trained exclusively on flat ground with at most 3 kg of added mass. Even so, the deployed real robot walked carrying an 11.5 kg payload (nearly equal to its own mass), stepped down unseen 16 cm drop-offs, and traversed five outdoor terrains including sand and rocky ground. Tracking errors were significantly reduced compared to baselines, beautifully combining control theory with RL adaptability.
contributions: Built a framework that lumps diverse uncertainties (payload variations, external forces) into a single joint disturbance, estimated online by a nonlinear disturbance observer without joint acceleration measurements.

Proposed a dual compensation pathway that uses the estimated disturbance for low-level feedforward torque compensation and as policy observation input, maintaining a consistent closed loop during both training and real-world deployment.

Developed a sensorless contact force estimator that reconstructs contact forces geometrically and dynamically from only joint states and IMU measurements, addressing the issue that many commercial robots lack foot force sensors.

sections.heading: Why combine explicit disturbance estimation with reinforcement learning now?
sections.summary: Domain randomization and adaptation modules have been used to improve quadruped robustness, but faced trade-offs with tracking precision and dynamics mismatches during deployment. PACE explicitly estimates disturbances for both torque compensation and policy observation, achieving zero-shot adaptation from flat-ground training to harsh real-world environments.
sections.details:
Quadruped robots possess mobility to traverse uneven terrain. However, to operate stably in real environments, they must withstand model uncertainties such as payload variations, external forces, and actuator degradation. Traditional model-based methods like model predictive control (MPC) rely heavily on precise dynamics models and meticulous parameter tuning. When actual robot characteristics deviate from design assumptions, performance drops significantly.

Meanwhile, deep reinforcement learning (RL) using simulators has achieved remarkable success. Mainstream robustness techniques in RL are domain randomization (DR) and latent representation estimation of environmental properties from response history (such as RMA). However, because these put all the burden on a single policy network channel, generalizing out-of-distribution (OOD) is difficult, and precise velocity tracking is sacrificed across conditions. Additionally, methods that retrofit disturbance adaptation modules after training suffer from an underlying dynamics mismatch between training and real-world deployment.

To address this, the authors proposed PACE (Policy Augmentation and Compensation with Explicit disturbance estimation), which treats various uncertainties collectively as an equivalent joint disturbance torque and explicitly estimates it using a nonlinear disturbance observer (DO). The estimated disturbance is first added to the joint PD controller as torque-level feedforward compensation, and is also passed to the policy as observation information. Keeping this observer in the loop during training allows the policy to act smartly from the start, assuming disturbances are already partially canceled.

Moreover, since the real robot (Lite3) lacks accurate foot force sensors, the authors built a sensorless contact force estimator that reconstructs contact forces from onboard joint encoders and IMU data. Consequently, a single policy trained exclusively on flat ground in simulation demonstrated carrying an 11.5 kg payload (nearly its own mass), negotiating 16 cm step-downs, and traversing diverse outdoor terrains on the real robot.

captions.F1: Zero-shot deployment of a policy trained exclusively on flat ground in simulation to unseen real-world terrains. (a) shows traversal on a walkway with uneven pavers, and (b) on a gravel road covered with pebbles. The robot stably navigates without breaking down under terrain disturbances underfoot.

sections.heading: Model-based control and RL adaptation: progress and gaps
sections.summary: Traditional approaches like MPC relied entirely on model accuracy, while recent RL methods leaned on black-box adaptation via latent representations. PACE stands out by feeding physically meaningful disturbance estimates into both torque compensation and policy inputs, integrating them into the loop from early training.
sections.details:
### II-A Model-Based Locomotion Control
Model predictive control (MPC) and whole-body impulse control (WBC) have provided transparent control rooted in physical laws. However, their performance depends on accurate robot inertial parameters and contact models. When carrying loads or slipping on the ground in the field, assumptions break down and require re-tuning. In PACE, model-based control does not take the lead; instead, the learned policy is the primary controller, and the model-based disturbance observer acts as an auxiliary module compensating for residual dynamics.

### II-B Learning-Based Policies for Generalization
Recent RL research predominantly uses domain randomization or techniques that estimate environmental latent codes from historical observations (such as RMA, DreamWaQ, HIMLOCO). However, these latent variables are abstract and lack physical units, so they cannot be directly added to joint torques. As a result, disturbance correction response speed is bound to the policy inference rate (usually around 20–50 Hz). PACE estimates an explicit disturbance torque with physical units ($\mathrm{N\cdot m}$), enabling high-bandwidth compensation.

### II-C Combining RL and Model-Based Adaptation
Approaches like RL2AC attach an adaptive controller as a plugin after training the policy, and other works insert physical filters downstream of the policy. However, because they attach the adapter after policy training, a dynamics gap emerges between the training and real-world environments. Furthermore, treating rapidly changing foot contact forces collectively as residuals causes estimation instability. PACE overcomes these issues by keeping the disturbance observer in the closed loop during training and explicitly separating contact forces as an analytical term.

sections.heading: POMDP formulation and basic quadruped dynamics models
sections.summary: Quadruped locomotion is formulated as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) with a teacher-student reinforcement learning structure. Rigid-body dynamics equations for the 12 robot joints and standard joint PD control architecture are also established.
sections.details:
### III-A Reinforcement Learning Formulation
We formulate quadruped locomotion as an infinite-horizon partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). On the real robot, the system can only directly observe an internal state vector $\mathbf{o}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{117}$, which excludes environmental parameters like ground friction or payload mass.

Therefore, we introduce an observation history $\mathbf{o}_t^H$ over the past $H=40$ steps, and a compressed latent representation $\mathbf{z}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{18}$ derived from privileged observation accessible only in simulation. During simulation training, a teacher latent $\mathbf{z}_t$ is generated from privileged information. During deployment, a student module (Adaptation Module) predicts an estimate $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_t$ from the observation history $\mathbf{o}_t^H$, adopting a two-stage knowledge distillation (Teacher-Student) structure.

### III-B Quadruped Dynamics and Low-Level Controller
Denoting joint positions, velocities, and accelerations for the 12 joints as $\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}, \ddot{\mathbf{q}} \in \mathbb{R}^{12}$, the joint-space equations of motion are expressed as:

$$\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}})\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{q}) - \mathbf{J}^\mathrm{T}\mathbf{F}_\mathrm{c} = \boldsymbol{\tau}$$

where $\mathbf{M}$ is the inertia matrix, $\mathbf{C}$ is the Coriolis and centrifugal term, $\mathbf{G}$ is the gravity term, $\mathbf{J}$ is the contact Jacobian, $\mathbf{F}_\mathrm{c}$ is the foot contact force vector across four legs, and $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ is the joint torque. Typically, the RL policy outputs desired joint positions $\mathbf{q}_\mathrm{des}$, which are converted by a joint PD controller into torque $\boldsymbol{\tau}_\mathrm{PD} = \mathbf{K}_\mathrm{p}(\mathbf{q}_\mathrm{des} - \mathbf{q}) - \mathbf{K}_\mathrm{d}\dot{\mathbf{q}}$ to drive the motors.

sections.heading: Inside PACE: fusing disturbance observers with sensorless contact force estimation
sections.summary: A nonlinear disturbance observer (DO) is designed to estimate deviations from nominal dynamics as lumped disturbances without acceleration measurements, distributing them to torque compensation and policy observation. For real-world deployment, a sensorless contact force estimator reconstructs foot contact forces from IMU and joint sensors, completing the observer inputs.
sections.details:
### IV-A Framework Overview
The overall PACE architecture is illustrated in Fig. F2. In parallel with the pipeline where the PD controller tracks joint targets generated by the learned policy, a nonlinear disturbance observer (DO) estimates the discrepancy between nominal dynamics and actual motion online as a lumped disturbance $\boldsymbol{\tau}_\mathrm{d}$. This estimate is directly added to torque as feedforward compensation, and simultaneously fed into the policy as an augmented observation.

### IV-B Disturbance Observer Design and Convergence
Individually identifying payload variations, CoM shifts, actuator degradation, and external pushes is difficult. Therefore, PACE treats them collectively as an equivalent joint disturbance $\boldsymbol{\tau}_\mathrm{d} \in \mathbb{R}^{12}$. To minimize computation and avoid configuration-dependent inertia calculation errors, the inertia matrix is approximated by a diagonal constant nominal matrix $\mathbf{M}$.

Because direct measurement of joint acceleration $\ddot{\mathbf{q}}$ is noisy, an acceleration-free nonlinear observer is constructed by introducing an auxiliary variable $\boldsymbol{\eta} \in \mathbb{R}^{12}$ and $\boldsymbol{\rho}(\dot{\mathbf{q}}) = L\mathbf{M}\dot{\mathbf{q}}$ (Eqs. 5, 6):

$$\dot{\boldsymbol{\eta}} = -L\boldsymbol{\eta} - L\left(-\mathbf{C}\dot{\mathbf{q}} - \mathbf{G} + \mathbf{J}^\mathrm{T}\mathbf{F}_\mathrm{c} + \boldsymbol{\tau} - L\mathbf{M}\dot{\mathbf{q}}\right)$$
$$\hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_\mathrm{d} = \boldsymbol{\eta} + \boldsymbol{\rho}(\dot{\mathbf{q}})$$

With observer gain $L > 0$ ($L=1$ in experiments), the error dynamics become $\dot{\hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}}}_\mathrm{d} = L(\boldsymbol{\tau}_\mathrm{d} - \hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_\mathrm{d})$. When the rate of disturbance change is bounded, estimation error is analytically proven to be uniformly ultimately bounded (UUB). Using this estimated disturbance, the control torque is compensated as $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \boldsymbol{\tau}_\mathrm{PD} - \hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_\mathrm{d}$.

### IV-C Sensorless Contact Force Estimator
Operating the observer requires the foot contact force term $\mathbf{J}^\mathrm{T}\mathbf{F}_\mathrm{c}$, but the real robot lacks force sensors. An estimator was designed to recover contact forces using only joint encoders and IMU data. Floating-base inverse dynamics (recursive Newton-Euler algorithm) computes model torques, yielding the residual torque against measured actuator torques: $\boldsymbol{\tau}_\mathrm{r} = \mathbf{J}^\mathrm{T}\mathbf{F}$.

To prevent numerical instability near contact Jacobian singularities, foot forces $\hat{\mathbf{F}}_\mathrm{raw}$ are computed using Damped Singular Value Decomposition (Damped SVD). Furthermore, unilateral contact conditions (no pulling force), normal force limits ($F_{z,\max}=300~\mathrm{N}$), and friction cone constraints ($\mu=1.0$) are enforced via a projection operator $\mathcal{P}_\mu$, followed by a low-pass filter ($\alpha_\mathrm{F}=0.35$) to obtain final contact forces $\hat{\mathbf{F}}_\mathrm{c}$. In MuJoCo validation, normal force RMSE against ground truth was $2.728~\mathrm{N}$, and joint torque error in the DO output averaged just $0.0542~\mathrm{N\cdot m}$, showing extremely high accuracy.

### IV-D Reinforcement Learning Framework
The policy is trained via PPO. Policy observations include base velocity commands, Euler angles, angular velocities, joint states, short history, and the explicit disturbance estimate $\hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_\mathrm{d}$. The action space consists of 12-dimensional joint target offsets from a nominal standing pose. The reward function adopts standard designs promoting velocity tracking, base stabilization, and smooth joint motions, training within a generic framework without custom reward tuning for the disturbance observer.

captions.F3: Foot vertical contact force estimation validation in simulation (MuJoCo). As shown in the zoomed top insets, delay is only 3 ms at touchdown and 9 ms at liftoff, demonstrating high temporal tracking, with vertical force root-mean-square error (RMSE) held to 2.73 N.
captions.F4: Comparison of disturbance observer output (rear-right Hip-X joint) between ground-truth contact forces and the proposed sensorless estimator. The waveforms overlap almost perfectly, and the error distribution on the right shows negligible discrepancy.

sections.heading: 11 dynamics variations, out-of-distribution commands, and extreme real-world tests
sections.summary: In simulation, PACE reduced velocity-tracking error by up to 57% across 11 dynamics variations and adapted immediately to unseen 2 m/s commands and 80 N lateral pushes. Real-world tests demonstrated carrying an 11.5 kg payload (near its self-mass), 16 cm step-downs, and traversing 5 outdoor terrains.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup and V-B Baselines
Training was performed in Isaac Gym with 4,096 parallel environments for 15,000 iterations. The real robot was a DeepRobotics Lite3 (mass ~11.6 kg), running the disturbance observer at a 3 ms control period (~333 Hz). Four methods were evaluated:
- **BASELINE**: Standard RL using RMA-style latent environmental factor estimation
- **HIMLOCO**: State-of-the-art method hierarchically estimating environment properties from internal robot responses
- **PACE 0**: Ablation using estimated disturbance only for torque compensation, omitting it from policy observations
- **PACE**: Full configuration using estimated disturbance for both torque compensation and policy observations

### V-C Experimental Results
#### 1. Velocity Tracking Under Dynamics Variations
Tested across 11 conditions including payloads (up to +6 kg), forward/backward/lateral CoM shifts, and actuator degradation (attenuation to 70%). Across the 11-condition average velocity tracking RMSE, PACE reduced error by 57.0% vs. BASELINE, 18.1% vs. HIMLOCO, and 32.8% vs. PACE 0, achieving the most accurate tracking across all conditions.

#### 2. Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Velocity Commands
When given a $2.0~\mathrm{m/s}$ forward command exceeding the training range of $[-1, 1]~\mathrm{m/s}$ (Fig. F6), BASELINE repeatedly fell. In contrast, PACE maintained stable locomotion with median tracking errors of just $0.11~\mathrm{m/s}$ (longitudinal) and $0.03~\mathrm{m/s}$ (lateral).

#### 3. Recovery From Instantaneous Lateral Push Disturbances
In a test applying an $80~\mathrm{N}$ lateral push for 0.48 s during forward walking (Fig. F7), recovery times were 300 ms for HIMLOCO, 204 ms for BASELINE, and 144 ms for PACE 0. PACE recovered in just **72 ms**—a 64.7% to 76.0% reduction in recovery time compared to baselines. The synergy of torque compensation and policy adaptation provides dramatic recovery.

#### 4. Real-World Step-Down Tests
In stepping down unseen drop-offs (8–16 cm), BASELINE failed upon landing at 14 cm and fell. PACE 0 cleared 14 cm, while full PACE cleared the maximum **16 cm drop-off** with a 100% success rate (Fig. F8(a)).

#### 5. Real-World Maximum Payload Tests
Incrementally adding payload, BASELINE failed at 8 kg (max 7.5 kg), and PACE 0 reached 11 kg. PACE continued to walk stably carrying **11.5 kg**—nearly equal to its own body weight (11.6 kg) (Fig. F8(b)). Since domain randomization during training only added at most 3 kg, this is a remarkable zero-shot adaptation far beyond the training distribution.

#### 6. Unseen Outdoor Terrain Tests
Traversability was tested across five outdoor terrains: pavers, lawn, sand, gravel, and large rocks (Table V). Despite flat-ground-only training, while BASELINE stumbled and fell on multiple terrains, PACE and PACE 0 achieved high completion rates between 80% and 100% across all surfaces.

captions.F6: Raincloud plots of velocity-tracking error distribution under an OOD velocity command of 2.0 m/s, far exceeding the training range (up to 1.0 m/s). While BASELINE experiences falls with a broad heavy-tailed error, PACE (bottom, green) exhibits errors sharply concentrated near zero in both longitudinal and lateral directions.
captions.F7: Lateral velocity response waveforms when an 80 N lateral push force is applied for 0.48 s during walking. While HIMLOCO took 300 ms and BASELINE took 204 ms to meet the recovery criterion (dashed line) after disturbance removal, PACE recovered in just 72 ms, demonstrating remarkable recovery speed.
captions.F8: Extreme robustness evaluation on the real robot (Lite3). (a) In step-down tests, BASELINE failed at 14 cm and PACE 0 fell at 16 cm, while only PACE successfully stepped down the 16 cm drop. (b) In payload tests, PACE maintained stable walking even while carrying an 11.5 kg payload, nearly equal to its own mass (~11.6 kg).

sections.heading: Takeaways and future outlook: merging classical control clarity with RL adaptability
sections.summary: PACE demonstrated zero-shot adaptation to harsh real-world environments by explicitly estimating lumped disturbances and routing them to torque compensation and policy observations. Future directions include adaptive observer gains and extensions to humanoid robots and contact manipulation.
sections.details:
This paper proposed PACE, a locomotion framework that lumps unmodeled dynamics and unknown external forces into a single joint disturbance, estimated and compensated online by an acceleration-free nonlinear disturbance observer (DO).

Torque-level feedforward compensation pulls low-level dynamics back toward nominal behavior, while feeding the estimated disturbance as an augmented policy observation enables disturbance-aware high-level stepping motions. Furthermore, the sensorless contact force estimator allows conventional real robots without foot force sensors to run the exact same observer structure as in simulation.

A current limitation is that the disturbance observer gain $L$ is fixed as a constant ($L=1$) across all joints and situations. Future work will introduce adaptive gain mechanisms that balance disturbance tracking speed against sensor noise sensitivity depending on the situation. The authors also envision extending the PACE architecture to humanoid robots and contact-rich manipulation tasks.

sections.heading: Appendix: Signal processing for sensorless contact force estimation and the failure of direct acceleration estimation
sections.summary: This section covers implementation details of differential acceleration filtering and coordinate transformations in the contact force estimator. It also presents a comparative experiment where disturbances were directly calculated from reconstructed accelerations without an observer, which caused noise amplification and immediate falls on hardware.
sections.details:
### Signal Preprocessing for Contact Force Estimation
Joint accelerations $\ddot{\mathbf{q}}_k$ and base angular acceleration $\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{\mathrm{B},k}$ required for inverse dynamics are initially approximated by forward differencing of measured joint velocities and angular velocities. However, numerical differentiation severely amplifies high-frequency noise, so a low-pass filter (coefficient $\alpha_\mathrm{d}=0.45$) is applied for smoothing. Smoothed IMU translational and angular accelerations are transformed into the world frame, serving as initial boundary conditions for floating-base recursive Newton-Euler dynamics.

### Why Was an Acceleration-Free Disturbance Observer Necessary?
A natural question arises: "If accelerations can be computed from inverse dynamics, why not directly calculate disturbance torques from them and compensate without using an observer?" To address this, the paper evaluated a comparative hardware baseline that directly computed disturbances from reconstructed accelerations via inverse dynamics for feedforward compensation and policy observation.

Upon hardware deployment, this direct acceleration-based method suffered severe control divergence due to feedback loops of sensor noise and differentiation errors, immediately losing balance and falling. This failure confirms that PACE's two-stage noise mitigation architecture—using acceleration only as an intermediate variable for constrained contact force estimation while relying on an integral-type acceleration-free disturbance observer for disturbance estimation itself—was critical for real-world deployment.

takeaways: Instead of delegating everything to RL latent variables, explicitly estimating disturbance torques with physical units and feedforward-compensating the PD controller dramatically improves low-level responsiveness.

Rather than retrofitting a disturbance observer onto a pre-trained model, embedding it into the training loop from the start enables the policy to acquire natural, unforced behavioral strategies assuming compensated disturbances.

Even without foot force sensors, combining inverse dynamics using an IMU and encoders with damped SVD, friction cone constraints, and output filtering provides practically effective contact force estimation.
limitations: The disturbance observer gain $L$ is a fixed value ($L=1$) shared across all joints, without joint-specific tuning for the optimal trade-off between tracking fast impact disturbances and sensitivity to sensor noise.

The nominal inertia matrix $\mathbf{M}$ is heavily simplified as a diagonal constant matrix, risking that modeling errors exceed lumped disturbance bounds during singular poses such as extreme leg flexion.

In environments with continuous 3D irregular contacts like large rocks, adding disturbances to policy observations was reported to slightly degrade performance in some cases, indicating the need to adapt according to contact characteristics.
